title: A multi-ensemble mean-field reduction method for networks of globally coupled phase oscillators with arbitrary parameter distributions
authors: Richard Gast, Shotaro Takasu, Helmut Schmidt, Ann Kennedy
abstract: Understanding the dynamical properties of coupled phase oscillator systems with heterogeneous oscillator frequencies has been a long-standing challenge of complex systems theory. While the seminal work of Ott and Antonsen dramatically improved our theoretical understanding of coupled phase oscillators for a small family of oscillator frequency distributions, we here present a mean-field reduction method for arbitrary frequency distributions. Our method leverages the drastic dimensionality reduction obtained for Lorentzian frequency distributions, and combines it with a data-driven multi-ensemble approach. As such, the method renders the Ott-Antonsen equations directly applicable to empirical distributions of phase oscillator frequencies, often achieving a drastic dimensionality reduction and allowing to study real-world physical and biological systems by means of stability, sensitivity, and bifurcation analyses.
summary: This paper presents a novel Lorentzian Mixture Mean-Field (LMMF) method designed to analyze coupled oscillator networks whose natural frequencies follow arbitrary distributions. By approximating the true distribution as a sum of Lorentzians, it achieves significant dimensionality reduction while maintaining high accuracy compared to existing methods. This technique is successfully applied both to theoretical Kuramoto models and to analyzing complex electrophysiological data from real neurons.
main_problem: The primary challenge is understanding the complex dynamics of globally coupled phase oscillator systems when the intrinsic frequencies ($\omega_i$) are heterogeneous (arbitrary distributions). The goal is to achieve a low-dimensional mean-field description for such systems.
main_result: The authors introduce the Lorentzian Mixture Mean-Field (LMMF) method, which successfully extends dimensionality reduction techniques from simple frequency distributions (like Lorentzian) to arbitrary empirical distributions by approximating them as mixtures of Lorentzians.
method: The core method involves approximating an arbitrary probability distribution $ho(\omega)$ using a finite sum of Lorentzian functions ($ho_M^*(\omega)$). This approximation is then used within the LMMF framework to derive low-dimensional mean-field equations for system observables like average phase coherence $R(t)$.
model_or_system: The model studied is globally coupled phase oscillators (e.g., Kuramoto models) and, in an application context, Quadratic Integrate-and-Fire (QIF) neural networks. Heterogeneity is introduced via the intrinsic frequency distribution $ho(\omega)$ or the distance-to-threshold $D_i$.
key_observables: Average phase coherence dynamics ($R(t)$), bifurcation structure (e.g., Hopf bifurcations, fold bifurcations), and steady-state firing rates.
important_parameters: The heterogeneity parameters defining the Lorentzian mixture components ($\mathbf{u}$ in Eq. 5) and global coupling strength $K$.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that an arbitrary distribution can be accurately approximated by a finite sum of Lorentzian distributions ($M$ ensembles). The LMMF derivation itself relies on mean-field approximations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the fitting performance of the LMMF model to empirical data (e.g., Gaussian mixtures for frequency distributions) and compare the resulting dynamics ($R(t)$) against previous theoretical approaches, showing superior accuracy and lower dimensionality.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general mean-field reduction technique by approximating arbitrary distributions as Lorentzian mixtures. It then applies this to Kuramoto oscillators, comparing LMMF results favorably against prior methods (Skardal's). Finally, it demonstrates the method's utility by applying it to analyze electrophysiological data from cortical neurons.
why_interesting: The development of a robust mean-field reduction technique applicable to arbitrary disorder distributions is highly valuable. While the system itself is classical/biological, the mathematical machinery (dimensionality reduction via spectral methods applied to complex systems) shares conceptual links with analyzing many-body quantum states or effective Hamiltonians in disordered quantum systems.
